As a lifelong resident of America's Wang, yes, many. It's generally fairly boring. Depending on the strength of the storm, you get a day or two of the most beautiful weather, followed by a day of sitting inside through ugly weather, followed by anything from a day, to a month or more, of clean-up.

Anything under a Category 3 is an excuse to skip work and have a hurricane party. Many people won't even bother to board up for a Category 1. When it gets up to Cat 2, you want to be wherever you're going before the storm gets really ugly, but it's still just a particularly wet and windy day off. Both of those will have some downed branches and flooding, maybe some non-native or unhealthy trees downed. Flooding, because everything is at sea level anyway. The surfing is great.

Once you get up to Cat 3, the locals start to take things seriously, instead of shaking their heads at the antics of storm virgins. Patios and yards are cleared, shutters are up, and people are ready to hunker down. Most folks will start to evacuate high risk areas, and they kick the tourists out of the Keys. The diehards, generally older, and in old houses (concrete block and rebar were popular in early 1900s Florida construction), will stick it out even in evacuation zones. There will be definite downing of trees and power lines. At Cat 4 and 5, you get significant damage, and probably loss of life. It was 2-3 weeks after Andrew, and a month after Wilma, before I had power back. You get real familiar with your generator.

All in all, it's entertaining to watch the uninitiated panic, the unprepared scramble, and the junior meteorologists get sent out into the ugliest part of the storm. You find ways to amuse yourself with close friends and family. If you're prepared, it's no big deal.

Many years ago, just after I'd moved to the Southern Hemisphere, I'd gone off for a few days sightseeing on my motorbike. I was about 500km (300mi) from home, and of course being on a motorbike I had no car radio, no regular news, since I was camping I hadn't watched tv for days (this was before smartphones too).. But I noticed a lot of people I met asked me if I was "worried about the Cyclone" or "getting ready for the Cyclone". Now, I didn't actually know what a Cyclone was, but I knew an Anti-Cyclone brought warm sunny weather, so I figured a Cyclone was probably the opposite. It couldn't be that bad, It wasn't like it was a Hurricane. But a lot of people seemed to be taking this whole thing quite seriously, so I decided that maybe I should ride home before it starts raining.

I was about 200km from home when it started raining. About 100km from home the wind started. I think the first indication I got that this wasn't a normal storm was when I realised I was leaning about 30 degrees into the wind just to keep my bike going in a straight line. It was about then I noticed that I was the only person on the entire motorway. The rain just got heavier and heavier, and every time there was a gust of wind I had to lean into it, as much as 40 degrees to keep the bike straight.

The part I remember most clearly was riding down a three lane motorway at about 90kph (55mph) in the left hand lane. Just as I passed the end of a row of trees that were sheltering me from the wind, a huge gust of wind hit me so hard I had to lean to over 45 degrees to keep a straight line. Unfortunately I think this had the effect of making my body and the motorbike act as a wing. I remember the feeling of rubber on road through the bike, stopped for a second or two, basically the wind picked me and the bike (240kg/380lbs total), up off the ground, and dropped me two lanes over in the right hand lane. I was a bit wobbly but I didn't come off.

Eventually, carefully, I got home. The next day it was still raining when I spoke to a few friends. I told them about my trip home the previous day. After looking at me like I was retarded for a few minutes, they gently explained that a Cyclone is what they call a Hurricane in the Southern Hemisphere. Apparently the one I rode through was a Category 2-3.
